title: Deodorant vs antiperspirant: how it works on your body
question: Do you use deodorant, antiperspirant, or both?
hook: Your deodorant might not be a deodorant.
lines: Your deodorant might not be a deodorant.
Check the label: lots are [antiperspirants](ˌæntipˈɜɹspəɹənts), or both.
Sweat itself barely smells.
Your armpits' [apocrine](ˈæpəkɹɪn) glands make an oily sweat.
Skin bacteria break it down, and that's the smell.
Deodorant fights the smell: it targets bacteria and adds fragrance.
[Antiperspirant](ˌæntipˈɜɹspəɹənt) fights the sweat.
Its aluminum salts [dissolve](dɪzˈɑlv) in your sweat.
They form soft gel plugs near the top of the duct.
Less sweat gets out.
The plugs wear away over time, so you reapply.
Tip: apply it at night, on dry skin, when you sweat least.
And no, research hasn't found a clear link to breast cancer.
Deodorant, [antiperspirant](ˌæntipˈɜɹspəɹənt), or both? Which do *you* use?

why: Sweat itself is odorless: underarm odor comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat from the apocrine glands, which sit in the armpits and groin and switch on at puberty (Cleveland Clinic; MSD Manual). A deodorant targets the smell: antibacterial ingredients and fragrance, but it doesn't stop sweat. An antiperspirant reduces sweat: its aluminum salts temporarily block the top of the sweat ducts with a gel plug (American Academy of Dermatology). The plugs wear away over time, so you reapply. In the US, antiperspirants are over-the-counter drugs, and many products are both (FDA). Dermatologists suggest applying it at bedtime on dry skin, when you sweat least, so it has time to work (AAD; Cleveland Clinic). The National Cancer Institute says no scientific evidence links antiperspirants or deodorants to breast cancer, and the American Cancer Society calls the evidence limited.
